children.text: GBIF and Wikipedia accept Anentome helena in the family Nassariidae. Wikipedia describes an 18–32 mm snail from Southeast Asia that spends much of its time buried in substrate and is carnivorous, feeding on worms and gastropods. The trade name “bumblebee snail” is also used for a marine species, so it is not a unique identifier.

Wikipedia says the species is carnivorous and feeds on worms and gastropods; the stored Carnivore diet is supported. LiveAquaria lists Omnivore, so the broader commercial classification is retained as a source disagreement. The snail is not a general community scavenger and can prey on small snails.

Aquarium Co-Op gives up to about 2.5 cm, 21–27 °C and pH 7.2–8.0; LiveAquaria gives 3 in / ~7.6 cm, 68–74 °F, pH 6.5–7.5 and moderate care. The stored 2.5 cm matches Aquarium Co-Op but conflicts with LiveAquaria; stored 20–28 °C and pH 6.5–8.5 span both sources and are retained as partial/conflict rather than averaged.

Wikipedia records Anentome helena as an intermediate host for Echinostoma revolutum and notes that uncontrolled sale could threaten native snails. That is a hygiene and release caution, not a treatment protocol. The stored Beginner difficulty conflicts with LiveAquaria’s Moderate rating and is preserved.

children.text: GBIF and WoRMS accept Astropecten polyacanthus. The stored scientific name matches the accepted name, but the stored “Beginner” difficulty is more optimistic than one source and the diet label is not consistent across sources. The record remains a single species; no subspecies or trade synonym is created.

Fast Aquatics gives 75–82 °F (about 24–28 °C), pH 8.1–8.4 and SG 1.023–1.025; Fishkeeping World gives 72–78 °F (about 22–26 °C) and pH 8.1–8.4. The stored 22–26 °C and pH 8.1–8.4 match one range and only partly match the other, so temperature is partial and pH is verified. No new salinity field is added.

Fast Aquatics describes a carnivore that feeds on small benthic invertebrates; Fishkeeping World labels it an omnivore. The stored Carnivore label is therefore supported by one source but contradicted by another, and the conflict is retained rather than averaged.

Both sources warn that this starfish exhausts the food in a sand bed and can starve slowly. A 55–75 gallon minimum and a mature system are practical requirements; no guaranteed survival time is asserted. Reef-safe status is reported as “with caution” because of its sand-fauna predation.

children.text: GBIF and Wikipedia accept Atya gabonensis. Wikipedia places it in West Africa from Senegal to the Democratic Republic of the Congo and gives 15 cm length. It is an omnivorous filter feeder that uses feather-like claspers; South American records are likely a different species.

Aquarium Breeder gives 22–28 °C, pH 6.8–7.2 (tolerance 6.0–8.0), GH 6–20 and KH 2–15; Aquarium Source gives 23–29 °C and pH 6.5–7.8. The stored 22–28 °C and pH 6.5–7.5 sit within those ranges and are verified. No GH/KH values are added to the record.

Wikipedia and Aquarium Breeder describe filter feeding on microorganisms and fine particles, with supplemental finely ground foods in captivity. The stored Filter feeder diet is supported. The tank needs established biofilm/plankton or supplemental feeding; no dose is asserted.

Both sources describe a peaceful, non-aggressive shrimp that hides during molting and benefits from moderate-to-strong current. The stored Peaceful temperament is supported. No universal community guarantee is made.

The stored Advanced difficulty conflicts with Aquarium Breeder’s easy-medium keeping rating, while breeding is described as very difficult. The record preserves that distinction: adult keeping is not the same as breeding.

The hobby sources describe an omnivore that grazes algae and biofilm and accepts prepared foods. The stored Omnivore diet is supported. No feeding dose is asserted.
Captive breeding is limited because the larvae require brackish or salt water. The record does not claim that the species breeds in a freshwater aquarium.

children.text: GBIF, WoRMS and Wikipedia accept Entacmaea quadricolor. Wikipedia places it in the tropical Indo-Pacific including the Red Sea, gives a diameter up to about 30 cm, and describes two growth forms and a symbiosis with several anemonefish species. It obtains energy from zooxanthellae and also captures food with its tentacles.

Aquarium Source gives 72–82 °F (about 22–28 °C), pH 8.1–8.4, dKH 8–12 and S.G. 1.023–1.025. The stored 24–28 °C and pH 8.1–8.4 are consistent; the source ranges are wider. These are hobby targets, not measured tolerances, and no salinity value is added to the record.

The stored Peaceful temperament is only partly supported: the anemone hosts anemonefish and does not chase fish, but it can sting and kill adjacent corals or other sessile invertebrates. It is not universally reef-safe and needs space and stable placement. No guarantee is made that a clownfish will accept it.

Wikipedia describes energy from zooxanthellae plus filter feeding and nutrients from anemonefish waste. Aquarium Source treats it as a carnivore that can take meaty foods. The stored Carnivore diet is therefore partial; no feeding schedule or dose is asserted.

Aquarium Source describes a humid setup with both land and shallow water; this is a terrestrial/freshwater crab, not a marine or fully aquatic species. The stored freshwater water type is therefore partial. No specific salinity or marine value is added.

The care source gives 70–82 °F (~21–28 °C), pH 7.5–8.0 and 0–10 dKH. The stored 22–26 °C and pH 7–8 are broader and partial. The stored 3 cm falls between the ~2.5 cm carapace and ~5 cm leg span, so size is partial.

The care source says vampire crabs can show aggression toward other creatures, while the stored temperament is Peaceful. That is a conflict and is retained. The crab also needs an escape-proof setup; no universal community guarantee is made.

children.text: GBIF, WoRMS and Wikipedia accept Hymenocera picta. Wikipedia places it on tropical Indian and Pacific reefs and notes that some authors split H. picta from H. elegans. It reaches about 5 cm and usually lives in pairs.

Wikipedia says the species feeds exclusively on starfish, including crown-of-thorns starfish, and prefers smaller sedentary starfish when available. It is not a general scavenger. LiveAquaria also lists Carnivore. The stored Carnivore diet is supported; no feeding frequency or starfish species is prescribed.

LiveAquaria gives 72–78 °F (about 22–26 °C), pH 8.1–8.4 and a maximum size of 1.5 in / ~3.8 cm. Wikipedia gives about 5 cm. The stored 24–28 °C is broader and partial; the stored 5 cm conflicts with LiveAquaria and is retained. pH 8.1–8.4 matches.

The stored Peaceful temperament matches the sources, but the shrimp will eat ornamental starfish and should not be kept with them. Reef compatibility is not a guarantee that it is safe with every echinoderm. No breeding guarantee is made.

LiveAquaria gives 72–78 °F (about 22–26 °C), pH 8.1–8.4 and a 2 in / ~5 cm size; Wikipedia gives 7 cm. The stored pH 8.1–8.4 matches, the stored 22–28 °C is broader and is partially supported, and the stored 5 cm conflicts with the 7 cm scientific description. No salinity target is added.

Wikipedia describes a cleaner shrimp feeding on parasites, necrotic tissue and detritus, and LiveAquaria lists Carnivore. The stored Scavenger diet is therefore partially supported rather than fully verified. The record does not claim that the shrimp will control Aiptasia in every tank.

The stored Peaceful temperament matches LiveAquaria. Reef compatibility is recorded as true, but it is not a universal safety guarantee: identification within the L. wurdemanni complex is uncertain, and individual shrimp may behave differently. No breeding or survival guarantee is made.

Wikipedia describes an elongated conical shell typically 20–36 mm (exceptionally up to 80 mm), a parthenogenetic and ovoviviparous life cycle, and a native range in northern Africa and southern Asia. Wikipedia says the snail feeds primarily on algae and detritus. The stored Omnivore diet is broader than that and is recorded as partially supported; the species is better described as an algivore/detritivore. No feeding dose is asserted.

Wikipedia states that M. tuberculata can carry trematode parasites and that 11 of the 37 listed trematodes are also human parasites. This is a reason for careful hygiene and against releasing snails into natural waters; it is not a diagnosis or a treatment instruction. Population control is also difficult because females reproduce parthenogenetically.

children.text: GBIF and Wikipedia accept Neocaridina davidi. Wikipedia places its native range in Taiwan, eastern China, the Korean Peninsula and Vietnam, and describes a 3–4 cm freshwater shrimp with a mottled brown wild type and many selectively bred colour morphs, including the red “cherry shrimp”. It has become invasive in some thermally polluted waterways through released captive stock.

LiveAquaria gives pH 6.6–7.0 and 60–80 °F (about 16–27 °C); the Aquarium Co-Op guide describes the species as widely adaptable. The stored pH 6.5–8 and temperature 20–28 °C are broader than the LiveAquaria values and are retained as partially supported rather than overwritten. These are commercial/hobby ranges, not measured tolerances.

Wikipedia and the Aquarium Co-Op guide describe an omnivore that grazes algae, biofilm, leftover fish food and shrimp food. The stored Omnivore diet is supported; no feeding schedule or dose is asserted.

The stored Peaceful temperament matches the hobby sources. Small shrimp can still be eaten by larger fish, so “peaceful” is not a universal community guarantee. No copper or medication protocol is given here.

Wikipedia notes that the species formerly called P. bridgesii is now P. diffusa, and the Aquarium Co-Op guide says “mystery snail” covers both P. diffusa and P. bridgesii. The stored scientific name is retained, but the identification is marked partially supported because the trade name does not resolve to one species.

The Aquarium Co-Op guide describes mystery snails as scavengers that eat excess fish food, dead animals and dead leaves, and says they do not eat healthy plants like larger apple snails. The stored Herbivore diet conflicts with that scavenging/omnivorous description and is retained as a conflict. No feeding dose is asserted.
The guide gives about 5 cm diameter, 21–26 °C and pH at least 7.2. The stored 5 cm size matches; the stored 20–28 °C and pH 7–8.5 are broader and are partially supported. No GH target is added.
The stored Peaceful temperament is consistent with the hobby source. Snails are sensitive to salt and copper-based medications; no treatment protocol is given here.

The trade name “Blue Crayfish” is ambiguous: the care source found here describes Procambarus alleni / Blue Florida Crayfish, not P. clarkii. The stored scientific name is retained, but the identification is partial.

The stored group is “shrimp”, while the animal is a crayfish; that grouping is recorded as a conflict rather than silently changed. Crayfish are predatory and can escape; the invasive status means they must not be released into natural waters. The source does not establish a community-safe temperament.

The available care page is for P. alleni, so its temperature, pH, size, diet, temperament and difficulty values are not applied to P. clarkii. Those claims remain NEEDS_EVIDENCE. Escape prevention and non-release are the evidence-supported cautions.

children.text: GBIF, WoRMS and Wikipedia accept Sabellastarte magnifica. Wikipedia describes a Caribbean sandy-reef polychaete that lives in a leathery tube, reaches about 10 cm in body length and projects a crown up to 15 cm in diameter. It removes organic particles from the water.

Wikipedia describes filter feeding on organic particles. LiveAquaria’s generic feather-duster listing says Omnivore and medium waterflow. The stored Filter feeder diet is supported by the species source; the commercial “omnivore” label is broader. No feeding dose is asserted.

The stored Peaceful temperament matches the commercial profile. Feather dusters are sensitive to poor water quality and handling; the crown may be withdrawn or shed after stress. No guaranteed survival claim is made.

The stored group “other” is imprecise for a polychaete worm and is recorded as partial rather than silently changed. The LiveAquaria profile is a generic feather duster, not confirmed as S. magnifica, so its 7-inch radiole size and care values are used only as supporting context. The stored 8 cm is between the 10 cm body and 15 cm crown measurements, so size is partial.

children.text: GBIF, WoRMS and Wikipedia accept Tridacna maxima. Wikipedia places it in the Indo-Pacific, gives a shell typically not exceeding about 20 cm, and describes byssal attachment and a colourful mantle with zooxanthellae. It is CITES Appendix II listed in the trade source.

Reeflings says the species needs intense lighting, stable parameters and a minimum volume around 100 L, with S.G. 1.022–1.025 and pH 8.1–8.4. Saltwater Aquarium Blog gives a larger 55-gallon minimum and moderate care. These are hobby recommendations, not measured requirements; no calcium or alkalinity dose is added.

Wikipedia describes filter feeding and zooxanthellae; Reeflings calls it a planktivore whose zooxanthellae provide most nutrients. The stored Photosynthetic diet is therefore partial, not a complete feeding description. No phytoplankton dose is asserted.

The record’s group is stored as “other”, while the animal is a bivalve/clam; that grouping is recorded as a conflict rather than silently changed. Sources also disagree on difficulty (Advanced vs Moderate/Moderate-to-easy) and size (about 20 cm vs 30–40 cm claims). CITES/legal status and sensitivity to parameter swings are practical limitations.

children.text: GBIF and Tropica accept Staurogyne repens. Tropica describes a fresh green, compact, hardy foreground plant found in the Rio Cristalino in the southern Amazonas, 5–10 cm tall with small leaves. Its nearest aquarium relative is Hygrophila, but the compact low stature is distinctive.

Tropica recommends cutting off the longest upright shoots when planting; new horizontal shoots then form from the base and gradually colonize the gravel. At low light growth is more upright and fewer side shoots form. It lists medium growth and low CO2, matching the stored values, but low light conflicts with the stored Medium light. No PAR or CO2 concentration is asserted.

Tropica warns that the full identity of this moss is not yet established and that studies may place it in the family Isopterygium; the record keeps the GBIF name but does not treat the identification as fully settled.

Tropica says growth is horizontal and overhanging, like a mini version of Weeping moss, and that attaching it to branching wood or vertical rock shows it at its best; it is also useful for a moss wall or hiding equipment. It is described as easy with quite low demands, but good light and some added CO2 promote growth and branching. It lists low light, low CO2 and medium growth; the stored Low light and Medium growth match, while stored None CO2 differs from the Low category and is preserved.

children.text: GBIF currently treats Taxiphyllum barbieri as a synonym of Ectropothecium barbieri, which is added as an alias. The trade name Java moss is retained because hobby material is sold under it; the record does not silently replace the name. Tropica describes the ‘Bogor Moss’ form from South-East Asia as 3–10 cm thick and willing to grow on any surface.

Tropica lists low light and low CO2 and medium growth, and says the moss can be attached with fishing line or cotton thread until it grips, then pruned with scissors when too luxuriant. The stored Fast growth differs from the commercial Medium category and is preserved. The dense growth can shelter fry, but no temperature or pH value is asserted here.

Tropica says the plant is believed to originate from China and was distributed by Oriental Aquarium Plants; the page’s Origin field says Asia. That “believed” wording is kept rather than presented as a confirmed native range.

Tropica describes a fleshy, 1–3 cm hanging moss with teardrop-like bright green shoots, best attached to driftwood or roots because the drooping growth creates depth. It says the moss has low demands, is fast growing in the text, and should be pruned frequently with scissors; the growth-rate field says medium. The stored Slow growth differs from both and is preserved as a conflict. It lists medium light and low CO2; stored Low light is lower and is preserved, while stored None CO2 differs from the Low category.

children.text: GBIF treats Vesicularia montagnei as a synonym of Vesicularia vesicularis, which is added as an alias; the Christmas moss trade name is retained. Tropica describes a 1–3 cm Brazilian moss whose side-branch structure distinguishes it from ordinary Vesicularia dubyana and resembles fir branches.

Tropica says it is more demanding and grows more slowly than ordinary Java moss, attaches readily to roots and stones, and needs pruning to keep an attractive shape. It lists medium light, low CO2 and medium growth. The stored Low light conflicts with the source Medium category; the stored Southeast Asia region is replaced by the source’s South America because the existing value had no supporting evidence.

Stored water baseline: temperature 24 °C–28 °C; pH 6.8–7.8; GH 5 dGH–15 dGH. Treat these as the current husbandry reference, not an independently verified tolerance limit.

children.text: Tailspot Blenny (Ecsenius stigmatura) is a saltwater species in the family Blenniidae, grouped as Blenny. The stored record gives a Beginner care level, an adult size of about 6 cm, and a minimum aquarium volume of 60 L. The recorded origin is Western Pacific, Philippines to Indonesia.

The database lists an adult size of about 6 cm. This is the stored baseline; the measurement basis (standard length versus total length) is not recorded, so treat it as a practical aquarium figure rather than a verified maximum.
Temperament is recorded as Peaceful. Solitary. Typical water zone: Bottom.
Minimum recorded volume is 60 L. Recorded aquarium styles: Mixed Reef. These are stored requirements; confirm footprint and filtration with the linked equipment records.
Stored water baseline: temperature 24 °C–28 °C; pH 8.1–8.4; GH 8 dGH–12 dGH. Treat these as the current husbandry reference, not an independently verified tolerance limit.
Diet is recorded as Herbivore. Offer a varied diet appropriate to that category; the record does not provide a verified feeding schedule or ration.
Temperament: Peaceful. Adult size: about 6 cm. Water type: saltwater. Water zone: Bottom. Use the linked compatibility records as the primary reference; a single label is not proof of compatibility.

children.text: Lawnmower Blenny (Salarias fasciatus) is a saltwater species in the family Blenniidae, grouped as Blenny. The stored record gives a Beginner care level, an adult size of about 13 cm, and a minimum aquarium volume of 100 L. The recorded origin is Indo-Pacific, Red Sea to Australia.

The database lists an adult size of about 13 cm. This is the stored baseline; the measurement basis (standard length versus total length) is not recorded, so treat it as a practical aquarium figure rather than a verified maximum.
Temperament is recorded as Peaceful. Solitary. Typical water zone: Bottom.
Minimum recorded volume is 100 L. Recorded aquarium styles: Mixed Reef. These are stored requirements; confirm footprint and filtration with the linked equipment records.
Stored water baseline: temperature 24 °C–28 °C; pH 8.1–8.4; GH 8 dGH–12 dGH. Treat these as the current husbandry reference, not an independently verified tolerance limit.
Diet is recorded as Herbivore. Offer a varied diet appropriate to that category; the record does not provide a verified feeding schedule or ration.
Temperament: Peaceful. Adult size: about 13 cm. Water type: saltwater. Water zone: Bottom. Use the linked compatibility records as the primary reference; a single label is not proof of compatibility.
The record links 5 problem records. Use those linked pages for symptom and troubleshooting guidance; this overview does not assert a diagnosis.
